meta.title: Norwegian A1 Beginner
meta.subtitle: 500 words · both directions, as two cards per word
meta.desc: Both study directions in one deck: Norwegian → English (see the Norwegian, recall the meaning) and English → Norwegian (see an English meaning, recall the Norwegian). Each direction is a card of its own with its own schedule, so recognising a word and producing it are learnt separately. 500 words of Norwegian Bokmål — the written standard most Norwegians use — for a beginner, aligned to A1 of the Common European Framework of Reference, whose global descriptor begins 'Can understand and use familiar everyday expressions and very basic phrases aimed at the satisfaction of needs of a concrete type' — a learner here is able to introduce themselves and others, to ask and answer questions about personal details such as where they live, people they know and things they have, and to interact in a simple way provided the other person talks slowly and clearly and is prepared to help. WHERE THESE WORDS COME FROM, since it matters: Norway examines learners at these levels — Norskprøven and Bergenstesten — but neither was found to publish a word list, so this deck is not an examination's vocabulary and does not claim to be. It is assembled from two things that can be stated. 356 of the 500 come from a vocabulary written for the level's scope — greetings and politeness, introducing yourself, family, numbers, telling the time, days and months, food and drink, shopping and money, the home, the town and getting about, the body and feeling ill, the weather, colours, and the pronouns, question words, prepositions and little words every sentence is built out of — and the other 144 are the commonest remaining words of everyday Norwegian, taken from a frequency list built from film and television subtitles and counted by the WHOLE word, every form of a noun or a verb added together. The cards are dealt by that frequency, so the words you meet most often come first. The 171 nouns are printed with their article — en, ei or et, and en/ei where Bokmål allows either — because the article is the gender, which decides the noun's definite ending, the adjective's ending and the pronoun that stands for it, and they show their definite singular and their plural (bilen, biler); the 114 verbs show their present, past and past participle, the forms a Norwegian verb is learnt by (spiser, spiste, spist), and behind the All forms fold their imperative, passive and participles. Real example sentences come with 493 of the 500 words, three apiece for 482 of them, with the word picked out in colour and a speaker beside the sentence and the headword. Sources. Level: the Common European Framework of Reference (Council of Europe), global scale. Meanings, gender and forms: English Wiktionary, via the kaikki.org extraction (CC BY-SA 4.0). Frequency: a word list built from OpenSubtitles (hermitdave/FrequencyWords, CC BY-SA 4.0). Example sentences: Tatoeba (tatoeba.org), CC BY 2.0 FR.
